content: Progesterone (vaginal) is a steroid hormone approved by the FDA for use in supporting embryo implantation and early pregnancy by supplementing corpus luteal function as part of an Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART) treatment program for infertile women. Common adverse reactions include post-oocyte retrieval pain, abdominal pain, nausea, and ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome. The recommended dose of Endometrin is 100 mg administered vaginally two or three times daily, starting the day after oocyte retrieval and continuing for up to 10 weeks. The efficacy of Endometrin in women aged 35 years and older has not been clearly established, and the appropriate dose for this age group remains undetermined. Endometrin is available as a 100 mg vaginal insert, which is a white to off-white oblong-shaped tablet debossed with FPI on one side and 100 on the other. Endometrin is contraindicated in individuals with previous allergic reactions to progesterone or any of its ingredients, known missed abortion or ectopic pregnancy, liver disease, known or suspected breast cancer, active arterial or venous thromboembolism, severe thrombophlebitis, or a history of these conditions. Physicians should monitor for early signs of cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disorders, such as myocardial infarction, stroke, arterial or venous thromboembolism, thrombophlebitis, or retinal thrombosis, and discontinue Endometrin if any of these are suspected. Patients with a history of depression should be closely observed, and discontinuation should be considered if symptoms worsen. Endometrin should not be used with other vaginal products, such as antifungal agents, as this may alter progesterone release and absorption. Adverse reactions reported during clinical trials include vaginal irritation, itching, burning, discomfort, urticaria, and peripheral edema. Other expected side effects of progesterone therapy include breast tenderness, bloating, mood swings, irritability, and drowsiness. No formal drug-drug interaction studies have been conducted for Endometrin. Drugs that induce the hepatic cytochrome P450-3A4 system, such as rifampin and carbamazepine, may increase the elimination of progesterone. The effect of concomitant vaginal products on progesterone exposure from Endometrin has not been assessed. Endometrin is classified as Pregnancy Category C by the FDA. It has been used to support embryo implantation and maintain clinical pregnancy in one clinical study. Live birth outcomes included singletons, twins, and triplets, with some birth defects reported. The safety and effectiveness of Endometrin in pediatric patients have not been established, and it is not intended for pediatric use. Similarly, no clinical data are available for patients over the age of 65, and its efficacy in this population is unknown. Progesterone is a naturally occurring steroid secreted by the ovary, placenta, and adrenal gland. It transforms a proliferative endometrium into a secretory endometrium in the presence of adequate estrogen, increasing endometrial receptivity for embryo implantation and maintaining pregnancy once implantation occurs. Endometrin contains micronized progesterone and is supplied with polyethylene vaginal applicators. Each insert delivers 100 mg of progesterone in a base containing lactose monohydrate, polyvinylpyrrolidone, adipic acid, sodium bicarbonate, sodium lauryl sulfate, magnesium stearate, pregelatinized starch, and colloidal silicon dioxide. Progesterone is approximately 96% to 99% bound to serum proteins, primarily albumin and corticosteroid-binding globulin. It is metabolized primarily by the liver into pregnanediols and pregnanolones, which are conjugated to glucuronide and sulfate metabolites. These metabolites are excreted via the kidneys and bile, with 50-60% eliminated through the kidneys and approximately 10% through bile and feces. Only a small portion of unchanged progesterone is excreted in the bile. Nonclinical toxicity studies to determine the carcinogenic or mutagenic potential of Endometrin have not been performed, and its effect on fertility has not been evaluated in animals. A clinical study evaluating luteal supplementation during ART demonstrated that Endometrin was non-inferior to an active comparator in supporting implantation and early pregnancy in women under 35 years of age or with serum FSH levels less than 10 IU/L. However, in women aged 35 and older or with serum FSH levels between 10 and 15 IU/L, Endometrin did not meet the criteria for non-inferiority. Endometrin vaginal inserts are individually packaged in sealed foil pouches and should be stored at 20-25°C (68-77°F), with excursions permitted between 15-30°C (59-86°F). Patients should be informed of the importance of reporting irregular vaginal bleeding, the potential side effects of progesterone therapy, and the recommendation to avoid using Endometrin with other vaginal products. The interaction between alcohol and progesterone (vaginal) has not been established, and patients should consult their doctor regarding alcohol use while on this medication.
